body:
How Jainism became part of Gujarat's heritage

Jainism originated in ancient India and gradually spread to different regions, including Gujarat. Over many centuries, Gujarat developed important Jain pilgrimage centres, temples, libraries, artistic traditions and institutions of religious learning. This heritage grew through the combined contributions of Jain monks and nuns, householders, merchants, scholars, artisans and rulers.

Gujarat's Jain heritage is especially important because it connects religion with trade, temple architecture, manuscript preservation and intellectual activity. A temple was a place of worship, but its construction and maintenance could also support artists, stone carvers, religious teachers and the copying of manuscripts.

Basic Jain concepts needed to understand the heritage

The word Jina means a spiritual conqueror: a person who has overcome attachment and passions. Followers of the Jinas are called Jains. Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras, enlightened teachers who show the path to liberation. A tirthankara is understood as a spiritual guide who helps others cross the cycle of worldly existence.

The Tirthankaras most closely associated with major Gujarat pilgrimage centres are:

  • Rishabhanatha or Adinatha: the 1st Tirthankara, especially associated with Shatrunjaya near Palitana.
  • Ajitanatha: the 2nd Tirthankara, associated with the principal Jain temple at Taranga.
  • Neminatha: the 22nd Tirthankara, especially associated with Girnar and also worshipped at Kumbhariya.
  • Parshvanatha: the 23rd Tirthankara, associated with Shankheshwar.
  • Mahavira: the 24th Tirthankara, whose teachings contributed greatly to the historical spread of Jainism.

Ahimsa and the Jain community

Ahimsa means non-injury to living beings. It is central to Jain religious life. Other important Jain vows concern truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy and non-possession. Monks and nuns follow strict forms of religious discipline, while lay followers support religious institutions and practise Jain principles within household life.

Jainism gained significant support from trading communities. Merchants could maintain their livelihoods while providing food and other assistance to monks and nuns, sponsoring temples and supporting religious learning. This did not mean that every trader was a Jain or that Jainism was confined to merchants. Rather, trading communities formed an important part of its historical support base.

Three connected forms of Jain heritage

  • Religious and architectural heritage: pilgrimage hills, temple complexes, shrines and images of Tirthankaras.
  • Literary and educational heritage: Jain scriptures, works on grammar and philosophy, illustrated manuscripts and libraries.
  • Social and economic heritage: donations by merchants, support from rulers, temple construction and the work of skilled artisans.

These forms of heritage should be studied together without treating them as identical. For example, Valabhi is particularly important for the transmission of Jain texts, Shatrunjaya for pilgrimage and temple architecture, and Akota for early medieval Jain bronze sculpture.

Prelims focus

  • Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras.
  • Adinatha is the 1st, Ajitanatha the 2nd, Neminatha the 22nd, Parshvanatha the 23rd and Mahavira the 24th Tirthankara.
  • Ahimsa is a central principle of Jainism.
  • Trading communities were important supporters of Jain religious institutions.
  • Gujarat's Jain heritage includes pilgrimage centres, temples, manuscripts and sculpture.
  • Trap: Jainism did not originate in Gujarat; Gujarat became one of its important historical centres.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas,' printed pp. 69–70; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings,' printed pp. 88–89.]

pictures.caption: Jain religious life and merchant communities in medieval Gujarat.

title: Jainism in Gujarat: Religious Foundations and Historical Development

body:
Location and religious importance

Palitana is a town in the Bhavnagar district of Gujarat. The nearby Shatrunjaya hills contain one of Jainism's most important pilgrimage complexes. Palitana is the town associated with the pilgrimage, while Shatrunjaya is the sacred hill on which the principal temple complex stands.

The main temple at Shatrunjaya is dedicated to Rishabhanatha, also called Adinatha, the 1st Tirthankara. According to Jain religious tradition, the hill is sanctified by events associated with Adinatha. Such accounts explain its religious significance and should be understood as matters of Jain tradition rather than independently established dates in ancient history.

A complex of many temples

Shatrunjaya is not a single isolated temple. It contains hundreds of Jain shrines arranged in groups across the hill. The complex developed through successive periods of construction, addition and renovation. Its buildings therefore should not all be assigned to one king, patron or century.

Many of its temples are organised into enclosed groups called tunks. A tunk is a temple enclosure containing a principal shrine and smaller associated shrines. This arrangement helps explain why descriptions of Palitana refer both to individual temples and to larger temple groups.

The larger complex includes temple gateways, pillared spaces, carved stonework and numerous images of Tirthankaras. Temple construction and renovation relied on donations and the work of skilled craftspeople over a long period.

Pilgrimage and the surrounding town

For Jain pilgrims, climbing Shatrunjaya is a religious act associated with devotion and self-discipline. The hill continues to attract large numbers of visitors, particularly during important religious observances such as Kartik Purnima.

Pilgrimage also shaped the development of Palitana town. Visitors required accommodation, food and other services, creating economic activity around the sacred centre. This illustrates how a pilgrimage site could influence a settlement beyond the walls of its temples.

Distinguish the location from the sacred centre

Palitana is the town; Shatrunjaya is the sacred hill; Adinatha or Rishabhanatha is the Tirthankara principally associated with its main temple.

Historical significance

The significance of Shatrunjaya lies in the combination of religious continuity and accumulated architectural patronage. Its temples represent the efforts of many generations of Jain donors and artisans rather than one short construction campaign.

Shatrunjaya also demonstrates the importance of Gujarat in the wider geographical network of Jain pilgrimage. It is especially associated with the Shvetambara Murtipujaka tradition, although other Jain traditions are also represented in the wider pilgrimage landscape.

Prelims focus

  • Palitana is in Bhavnagar district, Gujarat.
  • The sacred hill associated with Palitana is Shatrunjaya.
  • The principal temple is dedicated to Adinatha or Rishabhanatha, the 1st Tirthankara.
  • A tunk is an enclosed group of temples or shrines.
  • Shatrunjaya contains hundreds of temples developed over many centuries.
  • Trap: Shatrunjaya at Palitana is not the same pilgrimage centre as Girnar near Junagadh.

[Sources: District Administration, Bhavnagar, Government of Gujarat, 'Palitana Temple,' consulted 18 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill,' About the Place, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture,' printed p. 95.]

title: Palitana and Shatrunjaya: The Major Jain Pilgrimage Centre

body:
Girnar: The centre associated with Neminatha

Girnar is a sacred hill complex near Junagadh in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat. It contains both Jain and Hindu religious sites. Its principal historical Jain association is with Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.

The Neminatha temple is a major part of Girnar's Jain temple group and is associated with medieval temple construction. According to Jain tradition, Girnar is closely connected with Neminatha's spiritual life and liberation. The religious association of the hill should be distinguished from the construction dates of its surviving buildings.

Taranga: The centre associated with Ajitanatha

Taranga, in Mehsana district, is another important Jain pilgrimage and architectural centre. Its prominent medieval temple is dedicated to Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara.

The principal Ajitanatha temple belongs to the 12th century and is commonly associated with the patronage of the Chaulukya ruler Kumarapala. Its surviving stone architecture is an important example of the religious building activity that flourished in medieval Gujarat.

The Taranga hills are also associated with Buddhist remains. This does not make the Ajitanatha temple Buddhist; the temple is a Jain religious monument. The distinction matters because different religious traditions may have occupied or revered the same wider landscape at different times.

Other important centres

Jain centreLocationPrincipal association
GirnarJunagadhNeminatha, 22nd Tirthankara
TarangaMehsana districtAjitanatha, 2nd Tirthankara
ShankheshwarPatan districtParshvanatha, 23rd Tirthankara
KumbhariyaNear Ambaji, Banaskantha districtGroup of Jain temples, prominently including Neminatha
BhadreshwarKutchHistoric coastal Jain pilgrimage and temple complex

Shankheshwar

The Shankheshwar Jain temple, situated in Patan district, is dedicated to Parshvanatha. It should not be confused with the temple of Ajitanatha at Taranga or the temple of Neminatha at Girnar.

Kumbhariya

The Kumbhariya Jain temples are located near Ambaji in Banaskantha district. The group is known for richly carved medieval stone temples, with Neminatha among its important religious associations. Kumbhariya demonstrates that significant Jain architectural activity was not limited to Saurashtra.

Bhadreshwar

Bhadreshwar, in Kutch, is an important historic Jain pilgrimage centre near the coast. Its temple complex has undergone reconstruction and renovation at different times. Claims that its original temple was built in a precisely known ancient year are not securely established; its significance can be understood without relying on such dates.

How to distinguish the centres

The easiest factual distinction is between place, district and Tirthankara. Girnar and Shatrunjaya are both major sacred hills in Gujarat, but they are associated with different Tirthankaras. Taranga and Shankheshwar are also important Jain centres, but their principal temple associations differ.

Prelims focus

  • Girnar is near Junagadh and is associated with Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.
  • Taranga is in Mehsana district and its principal Jain temple is dedicated to Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara.
  • Shankheshwar is in Patan district and is associated with Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara.
  • Kumbhariya is near Ambaji in Banaskantha district.
  • Bhadreshwar is a historic Jain pilgrimage centre in Kutch.
  • Trap: Neminatha is the 22nd Tirthankara, not the 2nd; Ajitanatha is the 2nd.

[Sources: Gujarat Tourism, 'Girnar Hill,' About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Taranga (Hill) Jain Temple,' About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026; District Administration, Patan, 'Shri Parsvnath Temple, Shankheswar,' consulted 18 November 2026; District Administration, Banaskantha, 'Kumbhariya Jain Temple, Ambaji,' consulted 18 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, 'Bhadreshwar Jain Tirth Derasar,' About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Patan as a centre of political and intellectual life

Anahilavada-Patan, also known as Anhilwara or Anahilapataka, was an important capital of the Chaulukya dynasty, commonly called the Solanki dynasty, in medieval Gujarat. Its importance extended beyond administration and royal power to scholarship, religious institutions and cultural activity.

During the 11th and 12th centuries, Gujarat experienced substantial temple construction and literary activity. Rulers, ministers, religious teachers and wealthy householders contributed in different ways. Royal patronage could provide resources or prestige to a scholar, while merchants and other donors might support temples and religious institutions directly.

Hemachandra: Jain scholar of the 12th century

Acharya Hemachandra was a distinguished Jain monk, grammarian, scholar and author associated with the Chaulukya court. He was respected for his learning during the reign of Jayasimha Siddharaja and became especially influential during the reign of Kumarapala.

Hemachandra's significance was not confined to writing religious texts. He contributed to the study of Sanskrit and Prakrit, grammar, literature and Jain thought. His scholarship made Gujarat an important centre of intellectual activity.

Important works

  • Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana: a major grammatical work associated with Hemachandra and the patronage of Jayasimha Siddharaja. It deals with Sanskrit and Prakrit grammar.
  • Dvyashraya: a literary work associated with both grammatical learning and the history of the Chaulukya rulers.
  • Yogashastra: a work associated with Jain religious and ethical teaching.

Scholar and patron are different roles

Hemachandra was the scholar and author; Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala were rulers associated with his career and patronage. A royal patron is not automatically the author of a work produced under his patronage.

Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala

Jayasimha Siddharaja was a prominent Chaulukya ruler who supported learning and recognised Hemachandra's scholarship. This scholarly relationship does not establish that Siddharaja himself adopted Jainism; he is generally associated with Shaiva religious traditions.

Kumarapala, who succeeded Siddharaja, is remembered for substantial patronage of Jainism and a close relationship with Hemachandra. Jain literary traditions describe Kumarapala's adoption of Jain beliefs. The precise nature and development of his personal religious affiliation are treated with some caution because medieval accounts differ. His association with Jain patronage is, however, a major feature of Gujarat's religious history.

The important Ajitanatha temple at Taranga is commonly attributed to Kumarapala's patronage. This connects Chaulukya royal history with a surviving Jain monument in northern Gujarat.

Why this connection matters

The relationship between Hemachandra and the Chaulukya court illustrates a wider feature of medieval Gujarat: religious scholars could contribute to literature and language studies while receiving recognition from political rulers. Jainism's cultural influence therefore extended beyond temples to grammar, education and historical literature.

Prelims focus

  • Anahilavada-Patan was an important capital of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty.
  • Hemachandra was a prominent 12th-century Jain scholar.
  • Hemachandra was associated with Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala.
  • Siddha-Hema-Shabdanushasana is associated with Hemachandra's grammatical scholarship.
  • Kumarapala is associated with Jain patronage and the Ajitanatha temple at Taranga.
  • Trap: Siddharaja's patronage of Hemachandra does not mean Siddharaja was a Jain ruler.

[Sources: Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, Chapter II, sections on Siddharaja Jayasimha, Kumarapala and Hemachandra, published 1896; C. B. Sheth, Jainism in Gujarat (A.D. 1100 to 1600), discussion of Hemachandra and the composition of Siddha-Hema, pp. 45–46; Gujarat Tourism, 'Taranga (Hill) Jain Temple,' About the Location, consulted 18 November 2026.]
